The Ubuntu Podcast: a thirteen-year run in British Linux audio

For thirteen years the Ubuntu Podcast was a fixture of the British free-software calendar, a weekly Thursday conversation that grew out of the Ubuntu UK Local Community Team and ran from a first episode in March 2008 to a final sign-off in September 2021.

An English show with a global audience

The programme began life as the Ubuntu UK Podcast, recorded by volunteers from the country's local community team, and it never lost that grounded, regional flavour even as its listenership spread well beyond Britain. The hosts spoke plainly and in a family-friendly register about the week just gone, picking apart community news, flagging upcoming events, championing a useful command-line tool or two, and reading out the listener feedback that arrived between shows. A Telegram group and a scattering of social accounts kept the conversation running in the gaps between episodes, so the audience felt less like passive listeners and more like a standing circle of friends.

From its eighth season the show dropped the regional qualifier and became simply the Ubuntu Podcast, a small rebrand that matched how far its reach had travelled. Episodes were gathered into seasons of roughly forty instalments each, and a typical episode ran for about half an hour with no advertising breaks to interrupt the chat. The signature theme was a 1927 recording, Crazy Words, Crazy Tune by the Savoy Havana Band, chosen partly for its jaunty charm and partly because it had long since fallen out of copyright, a fittingly open choice for an open-source show.

The presenters

The line-up shifted across the years, but the final five seasons settled on a trio of Alan Pope, Mark Johnson and Martin Wimpress. Earlier seasons featured Laura Cowen, Tony Whitmore, Ciemon Dunville and Dave Walker, and the guest chair welcomed a long roster of community voices including Joey Sneddon, Stuart Langridge, Joe Ressington and Laura Czajkowski among many others.

Alan Pope

Alan was the one constant, present for every single season. He came to Ubuntu with its very first Warty Warthog release, having run Red Hat and then Debian since his first brush with Linux in the mid-1990s. He became an Ubuntu member in 2006, served the UK team and several community boards, and worked as Community Manager and later Developer Advocate at Canonical before moving on to InfluxData.

Mark Johnson

Mark, also a Warty Warthog veteran, spent his working days on the Moodle virtual learning environment and brought a steady interest in gaming on Ubuntu to the microphone, a useful counterweight to the more administrative concerns of his co-hosts.

Martin Wimpress

Martin had used Linux since 1995 and likewise started with Warty Warthog, becoming an Ubuntu member in 2016. He led the Ubuntu Desktop team at Canonical as Director of Engineering before leaving the company in early 2021, and he is a lead developer of both the MATE desktop and the Ubuntu MATE distribution.

How the show was made

Production leaned on the same distributed, do-it-yourself spirit as the software it covered. Each presenter recorded their own audio at home in lossless FLAC using the Audio Recorder application, and the separate tracks were later stitched together. Sessions usually happened on a Tuesday for release on the Thursday, and in the later years two episodes were taped back-to-back in one evening and then published a week apart. Post-production in that final stretch was handled by Joe Ressington and paid for through a Patreon campaign that the listeners funded directly.

The finished show went out as MP3, with streaming options on Spotify and YouTube, and it had earlier been published in Ogg Vorbis until the close of series ten. All of the audio carried a Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike licence. On 9 September 2021 the presenters announced the end of the run, closing the book with the fourteenth season and leaving a back catalogue that lives on through YouTube and the Internet Archive.
